idiom_name: dict of handlers keyed by the discriminator, or an ordered (predicate, handler) table (match for structural cases)
implementation_notes: Python has no static dispatch on payload shape, so the router is a dict from the discriminator to its handler - or an ordered list of (predicate, handler) rows when rules test values (amount > 1000) - while the match statement (3.10+) covers structural cases over tagged dicts or dataclasses and needs an explicit wildcard case to have a fallback at all. The table is the routing rules artifact, which keeps the destination x rule matrix testable without a broker; framework routers (FastStream, Celery) dispatch by subject or queue name, which is destination-based, so content decisions stay in this dispatcher. Keep the table module-level and immutable when the router is called from several threads or tasks.
pitfalls: match without a wildcard case _: falls through silently (fall-through is not an error in Python), so the fallback branch is mandatory boilerplate in this idiom.
A dict lookup with a missing discriminator raises KeyError unless .get(key, fallback) is used - the routing failure then surfaces as an exception with no route context.
A route table mutated at runtime (register/unregister) races with worker threads; build it at import time and rebuild-and-swap if the rules must change.
